# AgenticRL: Agentic Reinforcement Learning with Self-Refinement for Complex UAV Navigation

Roohan Ahmed Khan    Yasheerah Yaqoot    Amir Atef Habel    Muhammad
Ahsan Mustafa    Dzmitry Tsetserukou

###### Abstract

Deep reinforcement learning enables autonomous robots to learn complex
navigation tasks, but still relies heavily on time consuming manual
reward design and fine tuning. Existing automated reward generation and
refinement methods reduce this effort, yet often lack task-level
behavioral diagnosis for directing subsequent reward revisions. We
introduce AgenticRL, a multimodal closed loop framework in which
role-specialized agents generate executable rewards, diagnose failures
of the resulting policies, formulate targeted refinement instructions,
and regenerate improved rewards. Before training, a task grounding stage
automatically selects a compatible action profile, together with its
observation and reward interfaces. Each generated reward is used to
train a policy using Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO), which is
subsequently evaluated under randomized conditions. Task-level
behavioral, geometric, and safety measurements are organized into a
structured diagnosis packet and jointly analyzed with the current reward
code, task specification, behavioral summary, and visual scene context.
Unlike one-shot reward generation, human-guided refinement, or broad
candidate search, AgenticRL uses automated diagnosis of the behavior
induced by a reward to direct its next revision. We evaluate the
framework across eight UAV tasks covering navigation, obstacle
interaction, trajectory tracking, agile manoeuvres, and cluttered
flight. Under the reported comparative evaluation, AgenticRL achieves
success rates of $`100\%`$ in racing and $`88\%`$ in cluttered
navigation, exceeding the strongest Eureka and Text2Reward baselines,
respectively. Reward refinement increases mean simulation success from
$`37.2\%`$ to $`96.4\%`$, while the resulting policies achieve a
collective real-world success rate of $`90.0\%`$ and a sim-to-real
accuracy of $`93.4\%`$.

## I Introduction

Unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) are increasingly used in inspection,
search and rescue, agriculture, and navigation in cluttered or GPS
denied environments. Reinforcement learning (RL) has shown strong
potential for UAV navigation and control \[[1](#bib.bib4),
[2](#bib.bib6), [3](#bib.bib5)\], but its performance remains highly
dependent on reward design. For complex robotic tasks, manually
translating desired behaviors into numerical objectives is difficult,
and poorly designed rewards can lead to unstable learning, unsafe
behavior, incomplete task execution, or reward exploitation. Existing
approaches based on demonstrations, preferences, or human
feedback \[[4](#bib.bib7), [5](#bib.bib8), [6](#bib.bib9)\] can reduce
manual reward engineering, but often require additional supervision or
task-specific data.

![Refer to caption](2606.03963v4/images/title_fig.png)

Fig. 1: AgenticRL framework for reward refinement and policy deployment.
A VLM agent generates task-specific rewards, evaluates trained policies,
and acts as an agentic critic by diagnosing policy behavior and refining
rewards across iterative improvement epochs. The final refined reward
produces the best policy, which is selected and deployed through agentic
decision making for sim-to-real drone navigation.

Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) and vision language
models (VLMs) have enabled automated policy and reward generation. Prior
work has explored language conditioned policy
synthesis \[[7](#bib.bib1)\], reward generation from task
descriptions \[[8](#bib.bib2)\], and iterative LLM-based reward
optimization \[[9](#bib.bib3)\]. However, generating a plausible reward
function does not guarantee that the resulting RL policy will exhibit
the intended behavior. Existing approaches commonly rely on one-shot
generation, reward statistics, or candidate search, rather than
explicitly diagnosing task-level policy failures and using behavioral
evidence to guide subsequent reward revisions.

To address this limitation, we propose AgenticRL shown in
Fig. [1](#S1.F1 "Fig. 1 ‣ I Introduction ‣ AgenticRL: Agentic Reinforcement Learning with Self-Refinement for Complex UAV Navigation"),
a multimodal closed loop framework for behavior-grounded reward
refinement in UAV reinforcement learning. Given a natural language task
specification, scene image, and observation definition, AgenticRL
generates an executable reward function and trains a policy in
simulation. The trained policy is then evaluated under randomized task
conditions to construct a structured diagnosis packet containing
task-specific behavioral and geometric evidence, such as failure stage,
collisions, dynamic goal error, manoeuvre completion, obstacle
clearance, goal progress, and recovery behavior. A multimodal analysis
agent jointly reasons over this evidence, the current reward code, task
specification, behavioral summary, and scene context to identify likely
reward design deficiencies and generate a targeted refinement for the
next iteration. Thus, AgenticRL closes the loop between the reward
function and the behavior it actually induces, rather than relying
primarily on one-shot generation or broad candidate sampling. The main
contributions of our work are:

- •
  A multimodal AgenticRL framework with role-specialized agents for
  executable reward generation, behavioral diagnosis, and targeted
  reward refinement in a closed loop.
- •
  An automated task grounding and configuration mechanism that maps each
  task to compatible simulation, observation, reward, controller, and
  action-profile interfaces before training.
- •
  A scenario registry that supports multimodal scenario recognition and
  automatic selection of trained policies for deployment.
- •
  Evaluation across eight UAV tasks with distinct behaviors and action
  profiles, including validation on a real world quadrotor platform.

## II Related Works

### II-A UAV Reinforcement Learning and Reward Design

Reinforcement learning has been widely studied for UAV navigation,
obstacle avoidance, trajectory tracking, and sim-to-real
control \[[1](#bib.bib4), [2](#bib.bib6), [3](#bib.bib5)\]. Prior work
has shown that reward shaping can improve learning efficiency and policy
performance \[[10](#bib.bib15), [11](#bib.bib21), [12](#bib.bib13)\].
However, these approaches still rely heavily on manually designed
rewards, hand-tuned coefficients, and task-specific engineering, which
becomes increasingly difficult for UAV tasks involving safety,
stability, and collision avoidance.

### II-B Language and Vision Language Models for Learning

Recent works have explored the use of LLMs and VLMs for robot learning
and reward generation. LLMs have been used for robot policy
synthesis \[[7](#bib.bib1)\], proxy reward
modeling \[[13](#bib.bib10)\], executable reward generation from
language \[[8](#bib.bib2)\], and learning rewards from natural language
feedback or demonstrations \[[14](#bib.bib26), [15](#bib.bib14)\].
Similarly, VLM-based methods use visual grounding to generate or
evaluate robotic rewards \[[16](#bib.bib11), [17](#bib.bib25)\]. While
these approaches reduce manual reward engineering, many rely on
demonstrations, symbolic abstractions, human feedback, or one-shot
reward generation rather than task-level diagnosis of the behavior
induced by a trained policy.

### II-C Agentic Learning Pipelines

Recent work on agentic reinforcement learning shows that LLM-based
agents can improve through feedback, reasoning, tool use, and iterative
refinement \[[18](#bib.bib16), [19](#bib.bib17), [20](#bib.bib18),
[21](#bib.bib19), [22](#bib.bib20)\]. Other studies investigate scalable
agentic RL systems and tool-augmented reward models for long-horizon
tasks \[[23](#bib.bib24), [24](#bib.bib23)\]. These methods primarily
target text-based or reasoning-oriented environments rather than
embodied UAV learning.

Among related automated RL frameworks, Agents
Trainer \[[25](#bib.bib12)\] automates parts of the MARL pipeline for
drone swarms using specialized agents for reward generation and
evaluation. However, it targets multi-agent training automation rather
than multimodal reward refinement driven by task-level policy behavior.
AgenticRL instead combines multimodal task grounding, executable reward
generation, structured behavioral diagnosis, and iterative reward
refinement for UAV policy learning, with validation across multiple
simulation and real-world scenarios.

Table [I](#S2.T1 "TABLE I ‣ II-C Agentic Learning Pipelines ‣ II Related Works ‣ AgenticRL: Agentic Reinforcement Learning with Self-Refinement for Complex UAV Navigation")
summarizes the main differences between AgenticRL and the most relevant
existing frameworks. Prior work has made substantial progress in robot
policy code generation, language guided reward synthesis, VLM-based
reward generation, and agentic RL pipelines. However, existing methods
usually address only part of the full problem. Some generate policy code
directly, some generate rewards from text, some use visual inputs only
for reward verification, and others automate MARL pipelines without
explicit visual scene conditioning. AgenticRL combines these directions
by generating reward code from language and scene context, training UAV
policies in simulation, diagnosing policy behavior, refining rewards in
a closed loop, and validating the learned policies on a real UAV.

|                  |             |              |                        |                     |                    |
| ---------------- | ----------- | ------------ | ---------------------- | ------------------- | ------------------ |
| Method           | Reward Code | Visual Input | Closed loop Refinement | Full Task Diagnosis | UAV Implementation |
| Code as Policies | ✗           | ✗            | ✗                      | ✗                   | ✗                  |
| Text2Reward      | ✓           | ✗            | Human-guided           | Limited Logs        | ✗                  |
| Eureka           | ✓           | ✗            | ✓                      | Reward Statistics   | ✗                  |
| Code as Reward   | ✓           | ✓            | ✗                      | Subtasks            | ✗                  |
| Agents Trainer   | ✓           | ✗            | ✓                      | Error Logs only     | ✓                  |
| AgenticRL        | ✓           | ✓            | ✓                      | ✓                   | ✓                  |

## III System Overview

### III-A Problem Formulation

We consider the problem of training reinforcement learning policies from
high level multimodal task specifications. Each task is defined by a
natural language instruction $`l_{0}`$, visual scene context $`I`$, and
an environment observation specification $`\mathcal{O}`$. The visual
context provides task relevant scene information, while $`\mathcal{O}`$
defines the state variables available to the policy and reward function.
Each task is formulated as a Markov decision process (MDP):

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

       ``` math
       \mathcal{M}=(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{A},\mathcal{P},R,\gamma),
       ```                                                          |     | (1) |

where $`\mathcal{S}`$ denotes the state space, $`\mathcal{A}`$ is the
continuous action space, $`\mathcal{P}`$ is the transition dynamics,
$`R`$ is the reward function, and $`\gamma`$ is the discount factor. The
policy $`\pi_{\theta}(a_{t}\mid s_{t})`$ maps observation
$`s_{t}\in\mathcal{S}`$ at time step $`t`$ to action
$`a_{t}\in\mathcal{A}`$, represented as either a velocity command or a
collective-thrust and body-rate command depending on the scenario. The
observation space contains the UAV state together with task-specific
quantities such as gate poses, obstacle locations, landing targets,
barrier information, or trajectory waypoints.

The reward function $`R`$ is not explicitly available and must be
inferred from the multimodal task specification. Since a semantically
plausible reward may still induce incomplete, unsafe, or unintended
behavior, AgenticRL first generates an executable initial reward:

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

       ``` math
       R_{0}=\mathcal{G}_{\phi}(l_{0},I,\mathcal{O}),
       ```                                             |     | (2) |

where $`\mathcal{G}_{\phi}`$ denotes the VLM agent. The generated reward
is then used to optimize the policy objective:

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

````math
\theta^{*}=\arg\max_{\theta}\mathbb{E}_{\tau\sim\pi_{\theta}}\left[\sum_{t=0}^{T}\gamma^{t}R_{k}(s_{t},a_{t})\right].
``` |  | (3) |

AgenticRL subsequently evaluates the policy behavior induced by
$`R_{k}`$ and uses this evidence to guide reward refinement.

### III-B AgenticRL Framework

The overall architecture is shown in
Fig. [2](#S2.F2 "Fig. 2 ‣ II-C Agentic Learning Pipelines ‣ II Related Works ‣ AgenticRL: Agentic Reinforcement Learning with Self-Refinement for Complex UAV Navigation").
AgenticRL consists of a one-time task grounding stage followed by an
offline role-based reward refinement loop. Task grounding defines the
language objective, representative scene, environment assets, diagnosis
specification, and task criteria, which are fixed before iterative
training begins. The refinement loop then performs reward generation,
policy training, randomized evaluation, behavioral diagnosis, and reward
regeneration until the success criterion is satisfied.

Given the multimodal task specification $`(l_{0},I,\mathcal{O})`$, the
initial reward design agent generates an executable Python reward
function $`R_{0}`$ containing task progress, safety, and completion
terms derived from the available observations. The reward is integrated
into a customized UAV simulation environment \[[26](#bib.bib27)\] and
used to train a Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) \[[27](#bib.bib22)\]
policy. PPO is adopted due to its widespread use in continuous UAV
control and drone-racing applications \[[28](#bib.bib29),
[29](#bib.bib28)\].

After training, the policy is evaluated over randomized simulation
episodes using task-specific behavioral and geometric metrics. These
measurements are organized into a diagnosis packet $`D_{k}`$ and a
derived position–behavior summary that capture where and under what
conditions the policy fails.
Fig. [3](#S3.F3 "Fig. 3 ‣ III-B AgenticRL Framework ‣ III System Overview ‣ AgenticRL: Agentic Reinforcement Learning with Self-Refinement for Complex UAV Navigation")
shows an abbreviated example from the flip-traversal task, including the
original diagnosis packet excerpt, the derived behavioral summary, and
the resulting structured analyzer output.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

$`\Longrightarrow`$

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

$`\Longrightarrow`$

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Fig. 3: Flip-traversal refinement example showing the diagnosis packet,
position-conditioned behavior summary, and multimodal analyzer output
used to guide reward refinement.

The diagnosis analyst agent uses this behavioral evidence, together with
the current reward, task specification, and visual scene context, to
identify likely reward design deficiencies and generate targeted
refinement guidance:

|     |                                                 |     |     |
|-----|-------------------------------------------------|-----|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       p_{k}^{\mathrm{ref}}=\mathcal{H}_{\phi}(D_{k}),
       ```                                              |     | (4) |

where $`\mathcal{H}_{\phi}`$ denotes the diagnosis and refinement prompt
operator. The resulting guidance is incorporated into the task context:

|     |                                                               |     |     |
|-----|---------------------------------------------------------------|-----|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       l_{k+1}=\Psi_{\phi}\left(l_{k},\;p_{k}^{\mathrm{ref}}\right),
       ```                                                            |     | (5) |

where $`\Psi_{\phi}`$ denotes the prompt update operator. The updated
context is then passed to the reward refiner agent together with the
previous reward and multimodal task information:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
R_{k+1}=\mathcal{G}_{\phi}\left(R_{k},\;l_{k+1},\;I,\;\mathcal{O}\right).
``` |  | (6) |

The refined reward is retrained and re-evaluated, closing the
behavior-grounded refinement loop. If the success criterion is
satisfied, the best retained policy is selected for deployment;
otherwise, the diagnosis and refinement cycle continues until the
maximum given iterations.

## IV Experimental Setup

AgenticRL is evaluated on eight UAV tasks spanning navigation, obstacle
interaction, trajectory tracking, motion generation, agile manoeuvring,
and cluttered flight.
Fig. [4](#S4.F4 "Fig. 4 ‣ IV Experimental Setup ‣ AgenticRL: Agentic Reinforcement Learning with Self-Refinement for Complex UAV Navigation")
provides a visual overview of all scenarios in simulation and, where
applicable, Gazebo or real world deployment.

![Refer to caption](2606.03963v4/uav_scenarios.png)

Fig. 4: Overview of the eight UAV evaluation scenarios. The top row
shows the corresponding PyBullet training environments, while the bottom
row shows representative Gazebo or real world realizations where
applicable.

### IV-A UAV Task Scenarios

Five scenarios use linear-velocity actions: dynamic goal, obstacle
avoidance and landing, trajectory following, barrier crossing and
landing, and circular motion generation. In the motion-generation
scenario, the policy receives only the UAV state, without a reference
trajectory, and learns to produce the desired circular flight behavior
directly from the task specification. Three additional agile scenarios,
including racing, flip traversal, and cluttered navigation, use
collective thrust and body-rate commands. These tasks evaluate the
reward design workflow across different UAV behaviors and control
abstractions; policy transfer between the two action profiles is not
assumed.

All policies are trained using PPO with fully connected networks and
$`\tanh`$ activations. We use 16 parallel environments, rollout length
2048, minibatch size 256, and clipping parameter $`\epsilon=0.2`$.
Scenario-specific training budgets and hyperparameters are summarized in
Table [II](#S4.T2 "TABLE II ‣ IV-A UAV Task Scenarios ‣ IV Experimental Setup ‣ AgenticRL: Agentic Reinforcement Learning with Self-Refinement for Complex UAV Navigation").
For comparative reward design experiments, all methods use identical
policy-optimization settings and a fixed PPO training seed within each
scenario. Each generated reward candidate is trained once before
evaluation.

|  |  |  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|
| Scenario |     Action profile |     Steps per reward  (million) |     Learning rate | $`\gamma`$ |     Entropy coefficient |     Episode horizon (s) |
| Dynamic goal | Linear velocities | 25 | $`1\!\times\!10^{-5}`$ | 0.990 | $`0.10\!\rightarrow\!0.001`$ | 25 |
| Obstacle avoidance and landing | Linear velocities | 50 | $`1\!\times\!10^{-5}`$ | 0.990 | $`0.10\!\rightarrow\!0.001`$ | 25 |
| Trajectory following | Linear velocities | 50 | $`1\!\times\!10^{-5}`$ | 0.990 | $`0.10\!\rightarrow\!0.001`$ | 25 |
| Barrier crossing and landing | Linear velocities | 70 | $`1\!\times\!10^{-5}`$ | 0.990 | $`0.10\!\rightarrow\!0.001`$ | 25 |
| Circular motion generation | Linear velocities | 70 | $`1\!\times\!10^{-5}`$ | 0.990 | $`0.10\!\rightarrow\!0.001`$ | 25 |
| Racing scene | Body rates and thrust | 10 | $`1\!\times\!10^{-5}`$ | 0.990 | $`0.010\!\rightarrow\!0.001`$ | 12 |
| Flip traversal | Body rates and thrust | 15 | $`1\!\times\!10^{-5}`$ | 0.995 | $`0.020\!\rightarrow\!0.002`$ | 15 |
| Cluttered scene | Body rates and thrust | 15 | $`2\!\times\!10^{-5}`$ | 0.995 | $`0.015`$ | 20 |

TABLE II: Scenario-specific PPO training settings across the two UAV
action profiles.

For all scenarios, $`\mathcal{A}=[-1,1]^{4}`$. Under the linear-velocity
profile, the first three action components define the desired direction
and the fourth scales the speed limit. Under the body-rate and thrust
profile, the first component controls collective thrust and the
remaining components scale roll, pitch, and yaw rates. The rate limits
are $`(5,5,4.5)`$, $`(6,6,5)`$, and $`(7,7,6.5)`$ rad/s for racing, flip
traversal, and cluttered navigation, respectively, with corresponding
thrust ranges of $`[0,2.5]g`$, $`[0,3]g`$, and $`[0,2.5]g`$.

GPT-5.6-sol with medium reasoning is used as the primary agent for
reward generation, behavioral analysis, and refinement, conditioned on
the task description, scene image, and observation specification. During
deployment, a lightweight VLM agent identifies the observed scenario and
selects the corresponding trained policy from the scenario registry.

Real world experiments are conducted on a physical quadrotor using ROS2,
an Orange Pi 8GB onboard computer, and an Intel RealSense camera, with
Vicon motion capture providing pose measurements for evaluation. The
learned policies are validated across two autopilot stacks: ArduPilot,
where velocity commands are transmitted through MAVROS at 25 Hz, and
PX4, where body-rate and collective-thrust policies are tested in a
Gazebo PX4 SITL environment using the uXRCE-DDS bridge and Micro
XRCE-DDS agent at 60 Hz. This validates that the same simulation and
training framework can support policies deployed through both higher
level velocity control and lower level body-rate/thrust control
interfaces.

### IV-B Evaluation Metrics

We report simulation success rate (SSR), real world success rate (RSR),
sim-to-real accuracy (S2R), and reward refinement gain (RRG). All eight
scenarios are evaluated over 100 simulation trials, while the five
linear-velocity scenarios additionally use 10 real world trials each.

For a given scenario $`s`$, the simulation and real world success rates
are defined as:

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\mathrm{SSR}^{(s)}`$ | $`\displaystyle=\frac{N_{\mathrm{sim,success}}^{(s)}}{N_{\mathrm{sim,total}}^{(s)}}\times 100,`$ |  | (7) |
|  | $`\displaystyle\mathrm{RSR}^{(s)}`$ | $`\displaystyle=\frac{N_{\mathrm{real,success}}^{(s)}}{N_{\mathrm{real,total}}^{(s)}}\times 100.`$ |  |  |

The collective success rate across all evaluated scenarios is computed
as:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathrm{SR}_{\mathrm{collective}}=\frac{\sum_{s=1}^{S}N_{\mathrm{success}}^{(s)}}{\sum_{s=1}^{S}N_{\mathrm{total}}^{(s)}}\times 100,
``` |  | (8) |

where $`S`$ denotes the total number of evaluated scenarios.

The simulation-to-real transfer accuracy for scenario $`s`$ is defined
as:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathrm{S2R}^{(s)}=\frac{\mathrm{RSR}^{(s)}}{\mathrm{SSR}^{(s)}}\times 100.
``` |  | (9) |

Reward refinement gain (RRG) measures the absolute increase in
simulation success rate between the policies trained using the initial
and final refined reward functions. For scenario $`i`$, it is defined
as:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathrm{RRG}_{i}=\mathrm{SSR}^{\mathrm{final}}_{i}-\mathrm{SSR}^{\mathrm{initial}}_{i},
``` |  | (10) |

and is reported in percentage points (pp). The collective reward
refinement gain is computed as the macro-average across $`M`$ scenarios:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathrm{RRG}_{\mathrm{collective}}=\frac{1}{M}\sum_{i=1}^{M}\mathrm{RRG}_{i}.
``` |  | (11) |

## V Results

### V-A Simulation-to-Real and Physical UAV Validation

Fig. [5](#S5.F5 "Fig. 5 ‣ V-A Simulation-to-Real and Physical UAV Validation ‣ V Results ‣ AgenticRL: Agentic Reinforcement Learning with Self-Refinement for Complex UAV Navigation")
summarizes reward refinement performance and subsequent transfer to the
physical UAV. Across the five real world tested tasks, the mean SSR
increases from $`37.2\%`$ with the initial rewards to $`96.4\%`$ after
refinement, corresponding to a collective RRG of $`59.2`$ percentage
points (pp). The refined policies achieve a collective RSR of $`90.0\%`$
and a collective S2R accuracy of $`93.4\%`$.

![Refer to caption](2606.03963v4/images/sim2real_training_summary.png)

Fig. 5: Simulation and real world success rates before and after
AgenticRL reward refinement.

The largest refinement gains occur in trajectory following and barrier
crossing and landing, where SSR improves by $`95`$ and $`93`$ pp,
respectively. Dynamic goal, obstacle avoidance and landing, and circular
motion generation improve by $`26`$, $`39`$, and $`43`$ pp,
respectively. Dynamic goal achieves perfect S2R accuracy, while
trajectory following retains $`94.7\%`$ of its simulation performance.
Barrier crossing and landing achieves an RSR of $`90\%`$ and an S2R
accuracy of $`96.8\%`$. Circular motion generation also achieves an RSR
of $`90\%`$, corresponding to an S2R accuracy of $`91.8\%`$. Obstacle
avoidance and landing exhibits the largest transfer gap, achieving an
RSR of $`80\%`$ and an S2R accuracy of $`83.3\%`$.

Representative physical flight trajectories are shown in
Fig. [6](#S5.F6 "Fig. 6 ‣ V-A Simulation-to-Real and Physical UAV Validation ‣ V Results ‣ AgenticRL: Agentic Reinforcement Learning with Self-Refinement for Complex UAV Navigation")
and
Fig. [7](#S5.F7 "Fig. 7 ‣ V-A Simulation-to-Real and Physical UAV Validation ‣ V Results ‣ AgenticRL: Agentic Reinforcement Learning with Self-Refinement for Complex UAV Navigation").
Fig. [6](#S5.F6 "Fig. 6 ‣ V-A Simulation-to-Real and Physical UAV Validation ‣ V Results ‣ AgenticRL: Agentic Reinforcement Learning with Self-Refinement for Complex UAV Navigation")
illustrates dynamic goal and circular motion generation, while
Fig. [7](#S5.F7 "Fig. 7 ‣ V-A Simulation-to-Real and Physical UAV Validation ‣ V Results ‣ AgenticRL: Agentic Reinforcement Learning with Self-Refinement for Complex UAV Navigation")
shows obstacle avoidance and landing, barrier crossing and landing, and
trajectory following. The resulting trajectories demonstrate that the
refined policies preserve the intended task behavior after deployment on
the physical UAV.

![Refer to caption](2606.03963v4/images/agentic_rl_2d.jpg)

### V-B Reward Refinement Dynamics

AgenticRL refines rewards by using the behavior induced by each
generated reward as feedback for subsequent iterations. These revisions
are not assumed to be monotonic; therefore, each generated reward is
evaluated through the policy behavior it produces, and the best
task-valid policy is retained.

To illustrate how the closed loop refinement dynamics operate,
Fig. [8](#S5.F8 "Fig. 8 ‣ V-B Reward Refinement Dynamics ‣ V Results ‣ AgenticRL: Agentic Reinforcement Learning with Self-Refinement for Complex UAV Navigation")
presents an example from the racing scenario. The initial reward
encouraged stable gate traversal but introduced a stationary hovering
behavior after the second gate. The diagnosis stage identified this
failure by analyzing task-specific behavioral evidence, revealing that
the policy satisfied intermediate objectives while failing to complete
the overall manoeuvre. Based on this evidence, the refinement agent
modified the reward structure by reducing excessive stability incentives
and introducing progress, crossing, and anti-stalling terms. The
resulting policy improved from $`0\%`$ to $`100\%`$ success rate while
reducing collision rate and gate-traversal error.

The overall refinement behavior across the three body-rate tasks is
shown in
Fig. [9](#S5.F9 "Fig. 9 ‣ V-B Reward Refinement Dynamics ‣ V Results ‣ AgenticRL: Agentic Reinforcement Learning with Self-Refinement for Complex UAV Navigation").
Racing reaches $`100\%`$ SR after the second reward, flip traversal
improves from $`50\%`$ to $`85\%`$ over three rewards, and clutter
reaches $`88\%`$ for the selected third reward despite an unsuccessful
intermediate refinement. These results indicate that AgenticRL can
improve policies through targeted reward revisions guided by
task-specific behavioral evidence, rather than relying only on broad
candidate generation or parallel reward search. By identifying failure
modes and adapting the reward accordingly, the framework focuses
refinement on the behaviors required for task completion.

hovered before the exit; targeted progress and anti-stalling terms
increased SR from $`0\%`$ to $`100\%`$ and reduced CR from $`6\%`$ to
$`0\%`$.

### V-C Comparative Analysis

Table [III](#S5.T3 "TABLE III ‣ V-C Comparative Analysis ‣ V Results ‣ AgenticRL: Agentic Reinforcement Learning with Self-Refinement for Complex UAV Navigation")
compares AgenticRL with Text2Reward \[[8](#bib.bib2)\] and
Eureka \[[9](#bib.bib3)\] under identical environments, foundation
model, PPO settings, and evaluation conditions within each task.
Text2Reward generates a single reward with optional human-feedback in
the loop, whereas Eureka searches three reward candidates per iteration.
AgenticRL instead trains one targeted reward proposal per iteration
using task-level behavioral diagnosis.

AgenticRL achieves the highest success rate in both evaluation scenes.
In racing, it reaches $`100\%`$ SR with $`0\%`$ collision rate and the
lowest gate error of $`0.116`$ m. In clutter, it achieves $`88\%`$ SR
with only $`1\%`$ collision rate. Eureka obtains slightly higher goal
progress and normalized area under the learning curve (NAUC) in clutter,
but with a substantially higher collision rate of $`38\%`$.

The API usage reported in
Table [III](#S5.T3 "TABLE III ‣ V-C Comparative Analysis ‣ V Results ‣ AgenticRL: Agentic Reinforcement Learning with Self-Refinement for Complex UAV Navigation")
reflects the different refinement strategies of each method. Text2Reward
requires fewer input and output tokens because it does not incorporate
detailed behavioral diagnosis or visual scene information. In contrast,
AgenticRL provides richer multimodal context, including task-level
behavioral evidence and policy failure analysis, resulting in higher
input token usage. However, this additional context enables targeted
reward refinement with fewer PPO trainings compared with candidate-based
search approaches. The output token usage remains comparable to Eureka,
indicating that the increased input context is primarily associated with
evidence gathering and analysis rather than substantially longer reward
generation.

| Text2Reward^(†) | 0.00% | 24.00% | 0.286 | 0.001 | 19.00% | 0.00% | 10.77 | 0.000 | 0.43/3.39 | 4.80/5.91 | 1/3 | 1/3 | 10/45 |
| Eureka^(‡) | 91.00% | 9.00% | 0.231 | 0.120 | 75.00% | 38.00% | 89.71 | 0.165 | 15.88/30.02 | 13.70/24.17 | 2/3 | 6/9 | 60/135 |
| AgenticRL | 100.00% | 0.00% | 0.116 | 0.579 | 88.00% | 1.00% | 87.85 | 0.152 | 110.95/403.12 | 9.54/25.61 | 2/3 | 2/3 | 20/45 |

TABLE III: Comparison of automated reward design methods on racing and
cluttered UAV tasks. API usage and search budgets are reported as
Racing/Clutter.

We further evaluate the racing policy, which is trained to traverse a
two-gate course in the nominal environment, without retraining by
increasing the course complexity. The Out-of-Distribution (OOD) courses
contain 3–10 gates arranged in closed loops with a smooth $`0.25`$ m
height variation and independently seeded $`\pm 0.10`$ m per gate height
perturbations.
Fig. [10](#S5.F10 "Fig. 10 ‣ V-C Comparative Analysis ‣ V Results ‣ AgenticRL: Agentic Reinforcement Learning with Self-Refinement for Complex UAV Navigation")
reports collision rate and mean flight speed over 20 matched seeds per
method and condition. AgenticRL maintains zero collision rate across all
OOD course lengths while preserving a stable flight speed, demonstrating
robust generalization beyond the two-gate training condition. In
contrast, Text2Reward and Eureka exhibit increased collision rates as
the number of gates increases, despite retaining higher flight speeds.

Fig. 10: OOD racing generalization from the two-gate training condition
to height-varying 3–10 gate courses without retraining. Error bars and
bands denote standard error over 20 matched seeds.

### V-D Foundation Model Sensitivity

Table [IV](#S5.T4 "TABLE IV ‣ V-D Foundation Model Sensitivity ‣ V Results ‣ AgenticRL: Agentic Reinforcement Learning with Self-Refinement for Complex UAV Navigation")
evaluates the effect of the underlying foundation model within the
AgenticRL pipeline on the racing task. GPT-5.6-sol and Gemini 3.1 Pro
achieve the highest performance, reaching $`100\%`$ success, while
GPT-5.6-sol obtains the highest NAUC of $`0.579`$. Gemini 3.1 Pro
reaches the success threshold after the initial reward generation,
resulting in a single iteration and lower token usage. The variation
across models highlights that the choice of foundation model influences
reward quality and refinement efficiency within the same AgenticRL
framework. Nevertheless, the pipeline remains applicable across
different multimodal foundation models, with performance differences
primarily reflected in the generated reward revisions.

### V-E Ablation Study

Table [V](#S5.T5 "TABLE V ‣ V-E Ablation Study ‣ V Results ‣ AgenticRL: Agentic Reinforcement Learning with Self-Refinement for Complex UAV Navigation")
evaluates the contribution of reward initialization, behavioral
analysis, and vision conditioning across the five linear-velocity
scenarios. The evaluated variants are defined as follows: zero-shot
reward generates a single reward directly from the task description
without refinement iterations; few-shot reward incorporates reward
examples and allows iterative refinement for up to two iterations; w/o
analyzer retains iterative reward regeneration but removes
analyzer-generated behavioral guidance; w/o vision removes scene images
while retaining textual and numerical feedback; and Full AgenticRL uses
visual context, behavioral diagnosis, and iterative reward refinement.
Zero-shot and few-shot reward generation achieve competitive performance
on selected tasks but remain inconsistent across scenarios. Removing the
analyzer substantially reduces performance, particularly for trajectory
following, dynamic goal, and barrier crossing, highlighting the
importance of behavior-grounded refinement. Removing vision conditioning
also degrades performance, especially in obstacle avoidance, barrier
crossing, and motion generation. Overall, the full AgenticRL framework
achieves the highest or joint-highest success rate overall.

|  |  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|----|
| Method |     Trajectory  Follow  SR (%) |     Dynamic  Goal  SR (%) |     Obstacle Avoidance  & Land  SR (%) |     Barrier Crossing  & Land  SR (%) |     Circular Motion  Generation  SR (%) |
| Zero-shot reward | 0 | 74 | 57 | 0 | 55 |
| Few-shot reward | 48 | 74 | 88 | 72 | 98 |
| w/o analyzer | 50 | 61 | 60 | 52 | 62 |
| w/o vision conditioning | 87 | 95 | 65 | 48 | 76 |
| Full AgenticRL | 95 | 100 | 96 | 93 | 98 |

TABLE V: Ablation study of AgenticRL across five scenarios.

## VI Limitations & Future Work

The framework introduces additional computational cost due to iterative
policy training and evaluation, as each refinement stage requires a new
reinforcement learning cycle before subsequent reward optimization. For
complex UAV tasks, a complete few-shot refinement process can therefore
require considerable training time.

Furthermore, although reward refinement is automated, some
environment-specific components still require manual specification,
including termination conditions, observation spaces, safety
constraints, and task configurations. Thus, a degree of task
customization remains necessary when extending the framework to new
environments. Finally, the evaluation is conducted in controlled
simulation and real world scenarios. While AgenticRL demonstrates
effective sim-to-real transfer, further validation in more diverse and
highly dynamic environments remains an important direction for future
work.

## VII Conclusion

In this work, we presented AgenticRL, a multimodal closed loop framework
for behavior-grounded reward generation and refinement in UAV
reinforcement learning. Rather than relying on one-shot reward
generation or broad candidate search, AgenticRL evaluates the behavior
induced by each generated reward, organizes task-specific behavioral,
geometric, and safety measurements into a structured diagnosis packet,
and uses this evidence to guide targeted reward revisions. The framework
additionally performs task grounding to select compatible action,
observation, and reward interfaces, and supports automatic policy
selection for deployment.

Evaluation across eight UAV tasks demonstrated the effectiveness of
AgenticRL across both linear-velocity and body-rate control settings,
supporting policies deployed through both ArduPilot and PX4-based
control stacks. Across the five real world validated tasks, reward
refinement improved the mean SSR from $`37.2\%`$ to $`96.4\%`$, with the
refined policies achieving a collective RSR of $`90.0\%`$ and S2R
accuracy of $`93.4\%`$. AgenticRL outperformed existing automated
reward-design baselines in comparative evaluations by using policy-level
behavioral evidence to guide targeted reward refinement rather than
relying only on one-shot generation or candidate search. The framework
remained applicable across different foundation models and evaluation
settings, demonstrating its flexibility for multimodal reward design.
Ablation studies further verified the contribution of behavioral
diagnosis and visual conditioning to reliable reward refinement.
